steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on using large language models for machine translation, where instead of translating directly the LLM post-edits NMT output at sentence and document level. Motivate the approach, explain its advantages including human-in-the-loop post-editing, and list our main findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs in NLP and their potential for MT
- LLMs for MT still under-explored; ICL and fine-tuning cost
- Parameter-efficient fine-tuning
- Our work: LLMs as automatic post-editors of NMT output
- Advantages: modularity, document-level coherence, human feedback
- Main findings and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs in NLP
  - explored for QA, dialogue applications (cite)
  - reach or surpass SOTA of traditional methods
  - shows general understanding, can process long inputs
  - inherently multilingual from web training -> may suit MT
- LLMs for MT under-explored
  - initial work at sentence and document level (cite)
  - still behind SOTA Neural MT (NMT) (cite)
  - mostly In-Context-Learning (ICL) (cite) because fine-tuning needs a lot of compute -> barrier to adapting LLMs for MT
- Parameter-efficient fine-tuning
  - Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) (cite) to overcome compute requirements -> new adaptation process
  - unclear if enough for adaptation and generalization
- Our work
  - LLMs for MT at sentence and document levels
  - ICL and parameter-efficient fine-tuning: adapters alone insufficient, may degrade (Section 4)
  - instead: Automatic Post-Editors (APE) correcting NMT hypotheses, not direct translators
- Advantages
  - modularity: SOTA or customized NMT applied independently, LLM improves after
  - LLM refines sentence-level NMT output; consistent, coherent text from fluent long-document generation
  - cascade allows human feedback: human-corrected previous sentences -> better current sentence; iterative, sentence by sentence (Figure 1, Iterative Manual Post-Editing)
- Findings
  - Effective combination of NMT and LLM: sentence-level LLM APE, big quality gains, robust even on out-of-domain test sets
  - Extension to document-level post-editing: gains in sentence- and document-level metrics; SOTA 88.7% on ContraPro English to German
  - Iterative manual post-editing: gold target context improves remaining translation quality at sentence and document level

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are being explored right now for many Natural Language Processing tasks, for example Question Answering and Dialogue Applications. They are even shown to reach or surpass the state-of-the-art performance of traditional methods. This shows that they have general understanding and can process long inputs. Because of these strengths, LLMs could also be suitable for Machine Translation (MT), since many of them are also inherently multilingual because they are trained on the web.

However, LLMs for MT are still an under-explored research area. There are initial works that use LLMs for MT at sentence and document-level, but the performance is still behind the current state-of-the-art Neural MT (NMT) methods.

These methods mainly use In-Context-Learning (ICL), because fine-tuning these models usually needs a lot of computational resources. So this could be a barrier to adapting LLMs for MT in an optimal way.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques like Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) were proposed recently to get around the large computational requirements. This makes a new adaptation process for LLMs possible. However, it is still not clear if these techniques are enough for successful adaptation and better generalization.

- Our work
  - LLMs for MT, sentence and document level
  - ICL + parameter-efficient fine-tuning: adapters alone insufficient, may degrade (Section 4)
  - propose LLMs as Automatic Post-Editors (APE) correcting NMT hypotheses instead of direct translators
- Advantages
  - modularity: SOTA/customized NMT independently, LLM improves after
  - refine sentence-level NMT output into consistent, coherent text (fluent long documents)
  - human feedback: human-corrected previous sentences improve current sentence; iterative, sentence by sentence (Figure 1)
- Findings
  - Effective Combination of NMT and LLM: sentence-level APE, big gains, robust out of domain
  - Extension to Document-level Post-Editing: sentence + document metrics improve; 88.7% on ContraPro English to German
  - Iterative Manual Post-Editing: gold target context improves remaining translation quality

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are being explored right now for many Natural Language Processing tasks, for example Question Answering and Dialogue Applications. They are even shown to reach or surpass the state-of-the-art performance of traditional methods. This shows that they have general understanding and can process long inputs. Because of these strengths, LLMs could also be suitable for Machine Translation (MT), since many of them are also inherently multilingual because they are trained on the web.

However, LLMs for MT are still an under-explored research area. There are initial works that use LLMs for MT at sentence and document-level, but the performance is still behind the current state-of-the-art Neural MT (NMT) methods.

These methods mainly use In-Context-Learning (ICL), because fine-tuning these models usually needs a lot of computational resources. So this could be a barrier to adapting LLMs for MT in an optimal way.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques like Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) were proposed recently to get around the large computational requirements. This makes a new adaptation process for LLMs possible. However, it is still not clear if these techniques are enough for successful adaptation and better generalization.

In this work we investigate using LLMs for MT at both sentence and document-levels. First we experiment with ICL and parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques to use the LLM for MT, and we find that just adding adapters is not enough and can even lead to degradation (Section 4). To fix this but still use the strengths of LLMs, we propose to adapt them as Automatic Post-Editors (APE) that correct the hypothesis of NMT systems, instead of using them as direct translators.

This approach has several advantages. It is modular, so state-of-the-art or customized NMT techniques can be applied independently, and then the LLM makes improvements on top. Also, LLMs can refine the output of sentence-level NMT systems and generate consistent and coherent text, using their ability to generate fluent and long documents.

The cascaded system of NMT and LLM is modular, and this also makes it possible to integrate human feedback. When we feed the LLM human-corrected translations of the previous sentences in the document, we show that it can use this feedback to improve the translation of the current sentence. In practice this can be done iteratively, sentence by sentence, while the annotator corrects the translated document step by step (see Figure 1 for Iterative Manual Post-Editing).

Our main findings and contributions are the following:

- • Effective Combination of NMT and LLM: Our sentence-level LLM APE successfully combines knowledge from NMT systems and LLMs, and this gives large improvements in translation quality. We also observe that the LLM APE is robust and can correct NMT systems well, even for test sets from other domains that it was not explicitly trained on.

- • Extension to Document-level Post-Editing: We extend the approach to document-level APE and see significant improvements in both sentence and document-level translation metrics. We get a state-of-the-art accuracy of 88.7% on the ContraPro English to German test set, which shows the effectiveness of APE.

- • Iterative Manual Post-Editing: We introduce a promising use-case scenario for iterative post-editing (shown in Figure 1). We show that giving gold target context improves the remaining translation quality a lot, at both the sentence and document levels, according to various metrics.

steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are being explored right now for many Natural Language Processing tasks, for example Question Answering and Dialogue Applications [1,2,3,4]. They are even shown to reach or surpass the state-of-the-art performance of traditional methods. This shows that they have general understanding and can process long inputs. Because of these strengths, LLMs could also be suitable for Machine Translation (MT), since many of them are also inherently multilingual because they are trained on the web.

However, LLMs for MT are still an under-explored research area. There are initial works that use LLMs for MT at sentence and document-level [5,6,7,8], but the performance is still behind the current state-of-the-art Neural MT (NMT) methods [9].

These methods mainly use In-Context-Learning (ICL) [10], because fine-tuning these models usually needs a lot of computational resources. So this could be a barrier to adapting LLMs for MT in an optimal way.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques like Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) [11,12] were proposed recently to get around the large computational requirements. This makes a new adaptation process for LLMs possible. However, it is still not clear if these techniques are enough for successful adaptation and better generalization.

In this work we investigate using LLMs for MT at both sentence and document-levels. First we experiment with ICL and parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques to use the LLM for MT, and we find that just adding adapters is not enough and can even lead to degradation (Section 4). The cascaded system of NMT and LLM is modular, and this also makes it possible to integrate human feedback. Our main findings and contributions are the following:

- • Effective Combination of NMT and LLM: Our sentence-level LLM APE successfully combines knowledge from NMT systems and LLMs, and this gives large improvements in translation quality. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are currently being explored for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as Question Answering and Dialogue Applications [1,2,3,4]. They have even been shown to achieve or surpass the state-of-the-art performance of traditional methods. This demonstrates their general understanding and their ability to process long inputs. Given these strengths, LLMs might also be suitable for Machine Translation (MT), as many of them are inherently multilingual from being trained on the web.

However, LLMs for MT remain an under-explored area of research. While there are initial works on using LLMs for MT at both sentence and document-level [5,6,7,8], their performance still lags behind the current state-of-the-art Neural MT (NMT) methods [9].

Notably, these methods mainly employ In-Context-Learning (ICL) [10], since fine-tuning these models often requires significant computational resources. This might therefore be a barrier to optimally adapting LLMs for MT.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques such as Low-Rank Adapters (LoRA) [11,12] were recently proposed to overcome these large computational requirements, enabling a new adaptation process for LLMs. However, it is still unclear whether these techniques are sufficient for successful adaptation and better generalization.

In this work, we investigate exploiting LLMs for MT at both sentence and document-levels. We first experiment with ICL and parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques to use the LLM for MT, and find that adding adapters alone is insufficient and may even lead to degradation (Section 4). To mitigate this while still exploiting the strengths of LLMs, we propose to adapt them as Automatic Post-Editors (APE) that correct the NMT system's hypothesis rather than as direct translators.

This approach offers several advantages. It introduces modularity, allowing state-of-the-art or customized NMT techniques to be applied independently, followed by improvements made by the LLM. In addition, LLMs can refine the output of sentence-level NMT systems and generate consistent and coherent text using their ability to generate fluent, long documents.

The modular cascade of NMT and LLM can also enable the integration of human feedback. By feeding the LLM human-corrected translations of previous sentences in the document, we show that it can leverage this feedback to improve the translation of the current sentence. In practice, this process can be applied iteratively, sentence by sentence, as the annotator progressively corrects the translated document (see Figure 1 for Iterative Manual Post-Editing).

We summarize our main findings and contributions below:

- • Effective Combination of NMT and LLM: Our sentence-level LLM APE successfully fuses knowledge from NMT systems and LLMs, leading to substantial improvements in translation quality. Importantly, we observe that the LLM APE is robust and can adeptly correct NMT systems even for test sets from domains it was not explicitly trained on.

- • Extension to Document-level Post-Editing: We extend our approach to document-level APE and observe significant improvements in both sentence and document-level translation metrics. Notably, we achieve a state-of-the-art accuracy of 88.7% on the ContraPro English to German test set, underscoring the effectiveness of APE.

- • Iterative Manual Post-Editing: We introduce a promising use-case scenario for iterative post-editing (as depicted in Figure 1). We show that providing gold target context significantly improves the remaining translation quality at both the sentence and document levels, as indicated by various metrics.
